lessons.title: Tawhid and its three categories
objectives: Define Tawhid and explain why it is the foundation of Islam
Describe tawhid ar-rububiyyah, al-uluhiyyah and al-asma wa’s-sifat
Apply each category to examples

keywords.def: affirming that Allah is One in His lordship, worship, names and attributes
Allah’s lordship: He alone creates, owns, sustains and controls
Allah alone deserves all worship
those who follow the Qur’an and Sunnah as understood by the Companions

starter: Write the shahadah in English and say what each half means.
Name three pillars of iman.
Recite and explain Surah al-Ikhlas.

teach.heading: Why begin with Tawhid?
bullets: Every prophet called people to worship Allah alone
“We sent to every nation a messenger: worship Allah” (16:36)
Everything else in Islam is built on this belief
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and a reminder of the shahadah. Explain that ahl as-sunnah wa’l-jama’ah learn their aqeedah from the Qur’an and Sunnah as understood by the Companions and the first generations (the Salaf). Ask: why does a building need a strong foundation?

teach.heading: Tawhid ar-Rububiyyah
bullets: Allah alone is Creator, Owner and Sustainer
“Allah is the Creator of all things” (39:62)
Many Makkan idol worshippers accepted this much
But accepting it was not enough to make them Muslim
teach.note: Qur’an 29:61 tells us that when the idolaters were asked who created the heavens and the earth they would say ‘Allah’. Ask: if they accepted that Allah is the Creator, why were they still wrong? Lead to the next slide: they worshipped others besides Him.

teach.heading: Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah
bullets: All worship is for Allah alone: prayer, du’a, trust, vows
“You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help” (1:5)
This is the meaning of La ilaha illa Allah
Prophets were sent mainly for this
teach.note: Define worship broadly: everything Allah loves from inner and outer deeds. Give a worked example: asking a doctor for treatment is fine because he is a means; asking a dead person or a statue to remove harm or give provision is shirk because it treats them as having Allah’s power. Check that pupils separate ‘asking within someone’s ability’ from ‘asking others for what only Allah can give’.

teach.heading: Tawhid al-Asma wa’s-Sifat
bullets: Believe in Allah’s names and attributes as He described Himself
“There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing” (42:11)
No likening Him to creation, no denying His attributes
We do not ask ‘how’; we believe as revealed
teach.note: Introduce the method of ahl as-sunnah: affirm what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ affirmed, without distortion, denial, asking how, or comparison. This is a short introduction only; we return to it in Year 9. Ask: which two things must we avoid? (comparing Allah to creation and denying His attributes).

teach.heading: Putting it together
bullets: Allah alone creates (rububiyyah)
Allah alone is worshipped (uluhiyyah)
Allah’s names and attributes are perfect (asma wa sifat)
teach.note: Use a quick sort activity: read statements and ask pupils to choose which category they belong to. Correct misconceptions. Close with du’a for firm tawhid.

practice: Sort these statements into the three categories: ‘Allah sends rain’; ‘I make du’a to Allah alone’; ‘Allah hears everything’.
Why was agreeing that Allah is the Creator not enough for the Makkan idolaters?
Explain the difference between asking a friend for help and worshipping something.
independent: Create a diagram of the three categories with a definition, a verse and an example for each.
Write a paragraph: ‘Why is Tawhid the most important belief in Islam?’
Write a short dialogue between two friends where one explains La ilaha illa Allah.
exit: Name the three categories of Tawhid and give an example of one.
lessons.homework: Write 150 words explaining the three categories of Tawhid to a younger relative.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-code the three categories and give sentence starters; stretch: explain why accepting Allah as Creator alone does not make a person a Muslim.

lessons.title: Shirk: the opposite of Tawhid
objectives: Define shirk and explain why it is the greatest sin
Give examples of major and minor shirk
Explain how a Muslim protects their tawhid

keywords.def: associating partners with Allah in His lordship, worship or attributes
showing off in worship so people will praise you
repentance: returning to Allah with sincerity
sincerity: doing deeds for Allah alone

starter: Name the three categories of Tawhid.
Give an example of tawhid al-uluhiyyah.
What does ‘La ilaha illa Allah’ mean?

teach.heading: What is shirk?
bullets: Shirk is giving to others what belongs only to Allah
Includes worshipping idols, graves, saints or the self
Also includes believing others share Allah’s power
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Be factual and calm. Define with a classroom example: if a pupil wrote someone else’s name on a prize that belongs to another, that is unjust. Shirk is the greatest injustice because it gives Allah’s right to someone else.

teach.heading: The gravest sin
bullets: “Indeed, shirk is a great injustice” (31:13)
“Allah does not forgive shirk, but forgives less than that for whom He wills” (4:48)
Ibn Mas’ud asked the Prophet ﷺ which sin is greatest: setting up a rival to Allah, though He created you (Bukhari, Muslim)
teach.note: Explain that 4:48 refers to dying upon shirk without repentance; anyone who sincerely repents before death is forgiven. Highlight the mercy of tawbah: Qur’an 39:53 tells us not to despair of Allah’s mercy and that Allah forgives all sins for the repentant. Ask: why is hope important here?

teach.heading: Major and minor shirk
bullets: Major shirk: praying or sacrificing to others besides Allah
Minor shirk: showing off (riya) in worship
Swearing by other than Allah is also warned against
Hidden desires to impress others can spoil good deeds
teach.note: Be careful: scholars of ahl as-sunnah divide shirk into major (takes a person outside Islam) and minor (a grave sin that does not). Riya is warned against strongly in authentic reports. Give Year 7 examples: praying nicely only when a teacher is watching; posting charity just for likes. Ask pupils for ways to renew sincerity.

teach.heading: Protecting our tawhid
bullets: Learn the Qur’an and Sunnah
Make du’a to Allah alone
Keep the intention pure: ‘for the face of Allah’
Avoid superstition, fortune-telling and omens
teach.note: The Prophet ﷺ warned against going to fortune-tellers (Sahih Muslim: prayer is not accepted for forty nights of the one who asks a diviner), a fact to share carefully. Ask: why do people believe in horoscopes? Stress that the future is known only to Allah (Qur’an 27:65). End with du’a for sincerity.

practice: Write a definition of shirk in your own words.
Decide: major or minor shirk? (a) praying to a statue (b) lengthening your prayer only to be praised.
Explain why tawbah gives hope even after serious mistakes.
independent: Write a leaflet ‘How to protect my Tawhid’ with five tips.
Explain in a paragraph why shirk is called a great injustice, using 31:13.
Write a sincere intention (niyyah) you can make before homework.
exit: Name one example of minor shirk and one way to avoid it.
lessons.homework: Write a short reflection on what ikhlas (sincerity) means for you in salah.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sorting cards for major and minor; stretch: discuss why sincerity affects whether good deeds are accepted.

lessons.title: Allah’s names and attributes: the way of the Salaf
objectives: Describe how ahl as-sunnah understand Allah’s names and attributes
Explain what is meant by the Salaf
Apply the method to simple examples

keywords.def: the pious predecessors: the Companions and the first three generations
attributes of Allah
likening Allah to His creation (not allowed)
denying or emptying Allah’s attributes (not allowed)

starter: Define shirk.
Name two types of tawhid.
Say two names of Allah and their meanings.

teach.heading: Who are the Salaf?
bullets: The Companions, then the Tabi’un, then their students
“The best of people are my generation, then those who follow them” (Bukhari, Muslim)
We follow their understanding of the Qur’an and Sunnah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. The hadith is narrated by Imran ibn Husayn and others, with the best generations in order. Ask: why would the Companions understand best? (They saw the revelation and lived with the Prophet ﷺ.)

teach.heading: Affirm without likening
bullets: We affirm what Allah says about Himself
We do not compare Him to creation
We do not deny the attributes revealed
We do not ask how: we trust Allah’s knowledge
teach.note: Use 42:11 as the key. Show two errors: ‘making Allah like creation’ and ‘denying the attributes out of fear of comparison’. Both are avoided by affirming with the verse’s balance. Example: Allah hears; His hearing is perfect and nothing like ours.

teach.heading: Examples from the Qur’an
bullets: Allah is Al-Hayy: the Ever-Living (2:255)
Allah is Al-Alim: the All-Knowing
Allah is Ar-Rahman: He shows mercy
He is Al-Aziz and Al-Hakim: Mighty and Wise
teach.note: Read Ayat al-Kursi (2:255) in English and highlight the names. The Prophet ﷺ said it is the greatest verse in the Qur’an (Sahih Muslim, Ubayy ibn Ka’b). Ask pupils which names they can find. Keep the explanation of every attribute simple at this stage.

teach.heading: Knowing Allah changes us
bullets: Knowing He sees us builds taqwa
Knowing He is Merciful builds hope
Knowing He is Provider builds trust
teach.note: Link each name to one behaviour (honest in exams, resilient in hardship, grateful for food). Ask pupils to complete: ‘Because Allah is ..., I will ...’.

practice: Name the two mistakes to avoid when speaking of Allah’s attributes.
Complete: Because Allah is As-Sami’, I will ______.
Who are the Salaf?
independent: Write a paragraph explaining 42:11 in your own words.
Make a table of five names of Allah, meaning, and how it changes your behaviour.
Create a short quiz of six questions on this lesson.
exit: What is the difference between tashbih and ta’til?
Why do Muslims follow the understanding of the Salaf?
lessons.homework: Learn Ayat al-Kursi with its meaning and find four names of Allah in it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: matching cards for terms; stretch: explain in writing why asking ‘how’ about Allah’s attributes is avoided.

lessons.title: Hira and the first revelation
objectives: Retell the events of the first revelation using the hadith of Aisha
Explain the first verses revealed
Describe the reaction of Khadijah

keywords.def: revelation from Allah to a prophet
the Night of Decree when the Qur’an began to be revealed
the cave on Jabal an-Nur where the Prophet ﷺ used to reflect
‘Read’: the first word revealed

starter: What does al-Amin mean?
Name the Prophet’s ﷺ first wife.
Name the angel who brought revelation.

teach.heading: Seclusion in Hira
bullets: Before revelation, the Prophet ﷺ had true dreams
He loved to spend time alone in the cave of Hira
He worshipped Allah and reflected
He was about forty years old
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and salawat. This account is in Sahih al-Bukhari from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her). True dreams came like the break of dawn. Ask: why might a person who saw injustice around him want time to think?

teach.heading: Jibril comes
bullets: The angel said, “Read!” (Iqra)
The Prophet ﷺ replied, “I cannot read.”
This happened three times
Then came the opening of Surah al-Alaq (96:1-5)
teach.note: Read 96:1-5 in English: ‘Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know.’ Highlight knowledge and the pen. Misconception: the Prophet ﷺ made up the Qur’an. Note that he was unlettered; the words came from Allah.

teach.heading: Khadijah’s comfort
bullets: He returned shaking: “Cover me!”
Khadijah said Allah would never disgrace him
She named his kindness, honesty and help to the needy
She took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal
teach.note: In Bukhari, Khadijah said: you keep family ties, bear the burden of the weak, help the poor, honour guests, and help those struck by calamity. Ask: what does her reaction teach us about being a supporter? Waraqah had knowledge of earlier scripture and said this is the same angel who came to Musa. Stress Waraqah was not the source of the Qur’an.

teach.heading: A new mission begins
bullets: Revelation paused, then continued
The Qur’an was revealed gradually over about 23 years
The first revelation took place in Ramadan, in the Night of Decree
“Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree” (97:1)
teach.note: Link to Edexcel passage 97:1-5: the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months. Ask: why would Allah choose a particular night? Keep the statement ‘in Ramadan’ (2:185) and ‘the Night of Decree’ (97:1) as the Qur’anic basis; do not give a specific date.

practice: Why did Khadijah say Allah would never disgrace the Prophet ﷺ?
Put the events in order: Hira, Jibril says Iqra, return to Khadijah, meeting Waraqah.
Which words of Surah al-Alaq mention knowledge?
independent: Write a diary entry of Khadijah on the night the Prophet ﷺ returned from Hira.
Create a captioned timeline of the first revelation using places (Hira, Makkah) and the words of the hadith.
Write three sentences on why the first revelation began with ‘Read’.
exit: What were the first words revealed?
What did Khadijah do to comfort the Prophet ﷺ?
lessons.homework: Learn the first five verses of Surah al-Alaq and their meaning.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequencing pictures and simplified text; stretch: explain how this event proves the Qur’an came from Allah and not from the Prophet ﷺ.

lessons.title: The call begins: from private to public
objectives: Name the first believers
Describe the stages of the call to Islam in Makkah
Explain the response of the Quraysh at Mount Safa

keywords.def: inviting people to Allah and to Islam
the hill in Makkah where the Prophet ﷺ made his public call
the Prophet’s ﷺ uncle who strongly opposed him
the house where early Muslims gathered

starter: What were the first words revealed?
Who comforted the Prophet ﷺ after Hira?
Name the angel.

teach.heading: The first believers
bullets: Khadijah was the first to believe
Ali, Zayd ibn Harithah and Abu Bakr accepted Islam early
Abu Bakr invited others such as Uthman, az-Zubayr and Talhah
The call was quiet at first
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Names as taught in the seerah. Ask: why would the Prophet ﷺ begin with those close to him? (They knew his character.) Dar al-Arqam was used as a meeting place, a detail widely found in the seerah.

teach.heading: The public call
bullets: Allah commanded him to warn his closest relatives (26:214)
He climbed Mount Safa and called the tribes
He asked if they would believe an army was behind the mountain
They replied that they had never known him to lie
teach.note: Narrated in Bukhari and Muslim from Ibn Abbas. Emphasise that the Quraysh affirmed his truthfulness. Then he said he was a warner of a severe punishment. Ask: why did he start with that question?

teach.heading: Abu Lahab’s response
bullets: Abu Lahab replied, “May you perish! Is this why you called us?”
Surah al-Masad (111) was revealed in response
Not all relatives opposed him; Abu Talib protected him
teach.note: Report this carefully; the surah condemns Abu Lahab and his wife. Teach that family ties did not decide the matter: guidance is from Allah. Ask: how did Abu Talib’s protection help the Muslims?

teach.heading: Core message of the call
bullets: Worship Allah alone
Believe in the Last Day
Be just, kind and honest
Leave idols and injustice
teach.note: Use a table comparing Quraysh habits (idols, burying girls, usury, tribal arrogance) with the new teachings. Mention that the Qur’an condemns burying baby girls (81:8-9). Ask: why did the message appeal to the weak and the honest first?

practice: Name three early believers.
Why did the Quraysh trust the Prophet ﷺ at Safa?
Why was Surah al-Masad revealed?
independent: Write the speech the Prophet ﷺ might have given at Safa using the hadith facts only.
Create a timeline of the first three years of the call.
Explain in a paragraph why the early Muslims kept the call quiet.
exit: Who was the first person to accept Islam?
What did the Prophet ﷺ ask the Quraysh at Safa?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph about why honesty mattered in the Prophet’s ﷺ call.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: speech bubbles for key moments; stretch: compare the private and public stages of the call.

lessons.title: Persecution and patience
objectives: Describe how the Quraysh persecuted the early Muslims
Retell the stories of Bilal and the family of Yasir
Explain how Muslims showed sabr

keywords.def: patience: steadfastness for Allah’s sake
being treated cruelly because of beliefs
a freed Abyssinian Companion, the first muadhdhin
an early martyr of Islam, may Allah be pleased with her

starter: Where did the Prophet ﷺ make his public call?
Who opposed him strongly in his own family?
What does da’wah mean?

teach.heading: Why did the Quraysh oppose Islam?
bullets: It challenged their idols and their trade at the Ka’bah
It said all people are equal before Allah
Their leaders feared losing power
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: who benefits from the old system? Make the link to wealth, pride and tribal leadership. Misconception: they opposed him because he was dishonest; they themselves had called him al-Amin.

teach.heading: Treatment of the weak
bullets: Slaves and the poor were tortured
Bilal was dragged on the hot sand and kept saying, “Ahad, Ahad”
Abu Bakr bought and freed Bilal
The family of Yasir were harmed; Sumayyah was killed
teach.note: Handle with care for age. Accounts of Bilal’s steadfast ‘Ahad’ (One) and Abu Bakr’s freeing him are in the seerah literature. Sumayyah is recorded as the first martyr in Islam. Ask: what gave them strength? (Belief in Allah and the Hereafter.)

teach.heading: The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ was mocked, insulted and abused
Khabbab complained of the hardship and was told to be patient (Bukhari)
They were told earlier believers suffered even more
teach.note: In the hadith of Khabbab (Bukhari) the Prophet ﷺ reminded them that earlier believers were sawn with saws, yet it did not turn them from their religion, and that Allah would complete this matter. Ask: how does that hadith give hope?

teach.heading: Sabr in action
bullets: Sabr is not weakness; it is strength
“Indeed, Allah is with the patient” (2:153)
Sabr includes staying firm, avoiding wrong, accepting what Allah decrees
teach.note: Link to the school context: bullying, difficult exams, family hardship. Ask: what is the difference between patience and giving up? Let pupils write one way they can show sabr this week.

practice: Give three reasons why the Quraysh opposed Islam.
Write one lesson from Bilal’s story.
Which hadith gave hope to Khabbab?
independent: Write a first-person account of Bilal’s steadfastness.
Make a chart: types of sabr (in worship, from sin, during hardship) with examples.
Write a short reflection on a time you needed patience and what helped.
exit: Name two Companions who suffered in Makkah.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about a time they showed patience, and write their story in 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-written sentence frames; stretch: contrast sabr with passivity using examples.

lessons.title: Migration to Abyssinia
objectives: Explain why some Muslims migrated to Abyssinia
Retell Ja’far’s speech before the Negus
Evaluate the importance of this migration

keywords.def: migration for the sake of Allah
the just Christian king of Abyssinia
the Prophet’s ﷺ cousin and spokesman
protection given to people fleeing danger

starter: Define sabr.
Who was Bilal?
Why did the Quraysh oppose Islam?

teach.heading: Why leave Makkah?
bullets: Persecution grew worse around the fifth year of the call
The Prophet ﷺ advised some Muslims to go to Abyssinia
A king there was known for justice
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. In the seerah the Prophet ﷺ said there was a king in whose land no one is wronged. Ask: what makes a safe place for believers? Note that the first group included Uthman and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet’s daughter.

teach.heading: The Quraysh send envoys
bullets: Quraysh sent Amr ibn al-As and another man with gifts
They asked the Negus to return the Muslims
He insisted on hearing the Muslims first
teach.note: Highlight the justice of the king: he would not judge without hearing both sides. Ask: why is that an important principle in Islam? (Link to fairness in court.)

teach.heading: Ja’far’s speech
bullets: Ja’far described life before Islam: idols, injustice, cruelty
He described the Prophet’s ﷺ truth, honesty and call to Allah
He recited the beginning of Surah Maryam
The Negus wept and refused to hand them over
teach.note: The narration is in Musnad Ahmad (Umm Salamah) and is graded hasan. Ask pupils to find the points Ja’far chose. Why would Surah Maryam be wise? (It honours Maryam and Isa, which Christians would appreciate.) Misconception: the Negus is not recorded to have publicly declared Islam during this event; many scholars hold that he accepted Islam later, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer for him (Bukhari and Muslim).

teach.heading: Lessons from Abyssinia
bullets: Muslims can live safely under a just ruler
Truthfulness and wisdom in speaking
Protecting faith matters more than comfort
Protecting those in need is a duty
teach.note: Ask: what would you say if asked to describe Islam to a stranger in two minutes? Let pupils draft a short speech in Ja’far’s style.

practice: Why did the Prophet ﷺ choose Abyssinia?
What did Ja’far recite to the Negus?
Explain one lesson about justice from the story.
independent: Write Ja’far’s speech as a 120-word script using the main points.
Make a map-based storyboard showing the journey from Makkah to Abyssinia.
Write a paragraph on the importance of honesty when explaining Islam to others.
exit: Who led the Muslim spokespeople before the Negus?
Give one reason why the Negus protected the Muslims.
lessons.homework: Prepare a one-minute talk ‘How would I explain Islam to a stranger?’
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: captioned sequencing frames and key vocabulary; stretch: compare Ja’far’s method of da’wah with modern ways.

lessons.title: What is hadith? The Sunnah and why Muslims need it
lessons.bigQuestion: The Qur'an tells Muslims to pray, but how would you know HOW to pray if you only had the Qur'an?
objectives: To understand what hadith and the Sunnah are and why Muslims need them alongside the Qur'an
successCriteria: All: define hadith and Sunnah correctly
Most: sort examples into sayings, actions and approvals
Some: use two ayat to explain why Muslims follow the Sunnah
lessons.crossCurricular: History: primary sources, as historians judge a source by who reported it and how close they were
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: love for the Prophet ﷺ and following his example

keywords.def: a report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did or approved
the way of the Prophet ﷺ: his sayings, actions and approvals
saying, action, silent approval
an excellent example to follow

hook.text: The Qur'an tells Muslims to pray, but how would you know HOW to pray if you only had the Qur'an?
hook.a: The Sunnah shows how: the Prophet ﷺ prayed and said 'pray as you have seen me pray' (Bukhari).

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah' (an-Nisa 4:80), and 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example' (al-Ahzab 33:21). The Sunnah is the second source of Islam after the Qur'an.

starter.q: What are the two main sources of Islam?
Which angel brought the Qur'an to the Prophet ﷺ?
Where was the first revelation?
Name one thing the Prophet ﷺ did that Muslims copy today.
starter.a: For example: saying Bismillah before eating, eating with the right hand, using a miswak

teach.heading: Hadith and Sunnah
bullets: Sunnah: the Prophet's ﷺ whole way of life
Hadith: a report that carries the Sunnah
Qur'an: Allah's words; Sunnah explains and applies them
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Make the distinction clear: hadith is the report; the Sunnah is the practice reported. (In fiqh, 'sunnah' can also mean a recommended act; here it means his whole way.) Ask for examples pupils already follow.

teach.heading: Three kinds of Sunnah
teach.note: Give each a simple example without claiming a number unless checked.

head: Kind
Meaning
Example
rows: 'Actions are only by intentions' (Bukhari and Muslim)
How he prayed and made wudu
A Companion's action he did not object to

teach.heading: Why Muslims need the Sunnah
bullets: Obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah (4:80)
He explains what was revealed (16:44)
He does not speak from desire (53:3-4)
Take what the Messenger gives you (59:7)
teach.note: An-Nahl 16:44: 'We revealed to you the Reminder so that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them.' Example: the Qur'an commands salah but the number of rak'ahs and the movements come from the Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ said 'pray as you have seen me pray' (Bukhari).

check.q: A Companion watched the Prophet ﷺ make wudu and copied it. Which kind of Sunnah is this?
check.why: It is something he did. Qawl is a saying, taqrir is approval of someone else's act; the Qur'an is Allah's revealed words.

teach.heading: Misconception
teach.note: Some people claim the Qur'an alone is enough. Show from the Qur'an itself (4:80, 59:7, 16:44) that the Qur'an commands following the Messenger, so rejecting the Sunnah means not following the Qur'an fully.

misconception.wrong: The Qur'an is enough; we do not need hadith.
misconception.right: The Qur'an itself commands us to follow the Messenger (4:80, 59:7); the Sunnah shows how to live it.

practice.q: Sort: a) 'Pray as you have seen me pray' b) the way he made wudu c) Companions ate a food in front of him and he did not stop them.
practice.a: a) qawl (saying) b) fi'l (action) c) taqrir (approval)
practice.model: I do: a) has his words, so qawl. b) is something he did, so fi'l. c) others acted and he stayed silent and allowed it, so taqrir.

practice.q: Which ayah says 'Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah'?
Hadith or Sunnah: which is the report and which is the way?
practice.a: Hadith is the report; Sunnah is the way

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a paragraph: 'Explain why Muslims need the Sunnah as well as the Qur'an.' Use the frame Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.
independent.a: Point: the Sunnah explains the Qur'an. Evidence: 16:44 or 4:80. Explain: e.g. salah details come from the Sunnah. Link: so Muslims cannot practise fully without it.
independent.model: Teacher models: 'Point: Muslims need the Sunnah because it explains the Qur'an. Evidence: Allah says the Prophet ﷺ was sent to make clear what was revealed (16:44). Explain: for example ... Link: ...'

independent.q: Extend: give one more example where the Qur'an gives a command and the Sunnah gives the details.
independent.a: For example: zakah (the Qur'an commands it; the Sunnah sets the amounts) or Hajj (the rites).

independent.q: Stretch: what does 53:3-4 tell us about the Prophet's ﷺ words?
independent.a: He did not speak from his own desire; it was revelation, so his teaching is guidance from Allah.

exit.q: A hadith is ...
exit.a: A report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did or approved
options: A report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did or approved

exit.q: Taqrir means ...
exit.a: Silent approval

exit.q: Back to our ponder: how would you know how to pray?
exit.a: From the Sunnah: the Prophet's ﷺ example, reported in hadith.

keywords.def: intention: the purpose in the heart
sincerity: doing a deed for Allah alone
showing off: doing good so that people praise you
migration; here the move from Makkah to Madinah

hook.text: Two people give the same £10 to charity. Could one get a reward and the other get nothing? How?
hook.a: Yes: one gave for Allah and one to be praised. Actions are judged by intentions (Bukhari and Muslim).

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what they intended' (Bukhari and Muslim, narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab). إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ

starter.q: Name the four main grades of hadith.
Mawdu' means ...
Which book begins with the hadith on intentions?
What is the matn?

teach.heading: The hadith
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Read it twice, slowly. It is the first hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari; we traced its chain last week. The second part mentions hijrah: the Companions who migrated for Allah were rewarded for that; someone who migrated for worldly gain or to marry got only that.

quote.text: Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what they intended. So whoever's hijrah was for Allah and His Messenger, his hijrah is for Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's hijrah was for some worldly gain, or a woman to marry, his hijrah is for what he migrated for.
quote.source: Umar ibn al-Khattab; Bukhari and Muslim

teach.heading: What is niyyah?
bullets: The purpose in the heart
Not words said aloud
Turns habits into worship
Must be for Allah alone (98:5)
teach.note: Al-Bayyinah 98:5: they were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion. Examples: eating to have strength for worship; sleeping early to pray fajr; studying to benefit the ummah.

check.q: Bilal helps his mum only so his friends see and praise him. What does he get, according to the hadith?
options: Only what he intended: the praise
check.why: 'Every person will have only what they intended.' His intention was praise, so that is all he gets. Changing the intention to please Allah would bring reward.

teach.heading: Same action, different reward
teach.note: Ask pupils for their own example before revealing the right column.

teach.heading: Intention is not enough alone
teach.note: Scholars teach that an accepted deed needs sincerity AND correctness (following the Sunnah). A good intention does not make a haram act halal.

misconception.wrong: If my heart is good, any action is fine.
misconception.right: A deed needs a sincere intention AND must be right according to the Qur'an and Sunnah.

practice.q: Turn this habit into worship by changing the intention: 'I go to bed early.'
practice.a: 'I go to bed early so that I can wake up for fajr and have energy to learn, for Allah.'
practice.model: I do: 1) Name the habit: going to bed early. 2) Ask: what good could it lead to? Praying fajr. 3) Add 'for Allah': 'I go to bed early so I can pray fajr on time, seeking Allah's pleasure.'

practice.q: Who narrated the hadith on intentions?
Riya' means ...

independent.q: In the portal response box, explain the hadith on intentions using PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. Use one example of your own.
independent.a: Point: actions are judged by intentions. Evidence: the hadith (Bukhari and Muslim). Explain: with an example such as charity. Link: Muslims check their intentions often.
independent.model: Teacher models: 'Point: In Islam, the value of an action depends on the intention behind it. Evidence: The Prophet ﷺ said, "Actions are only by intentions" (Bukhari and Muslim). Explain: ...'

independent.q: Extend: why do you think al-Bukhari began his whole book with this hadith?
independent.a: To remind the reader and himself to study for Allah; every action, including learning, depends on intention.

independent.q: Stretch: explain why a good intention does not make lying acceptable.
independent.a: Deeds must also be correct according to the Shari'ah; lying is haram whatever the intention.

exit.q: Ikhlas means ...
exit.a: Sincerity: doing it for Allah alone
options: Sincerity: doing it for Allah alone

exit.q: Back to our ponder: how could one giver get reward and the other nothing?
exit.a: Because one gave for Allah and the other for praise; each gets what he intended.

In Bukhari and Muslim: sahih
Islam pictured as a building
Five pillars hold it up
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Abdullah ibn Umar is the son of Umar ibn al-Khattab; do not confuse them. In this narration Hajj comes before fasting; in another narration in Muslim, fasting comes first.

teach.heading: The five pillars

What it is
Key fact

Due on savings above the nisab
Held for one lunar year

Missing one weakens the whole
Extra good deeds are like the walls and roof
The pillars shape character and community

practice.q: Calculate the zakah on £2,000 of savings held above the nisab for a lunar year.
Who narrated 'Islam is built on five'?
Which pillar is once in a lifetime for those able?

keywords.def: minor ablution
full bath for major impurity
dry ablution with clean earth when water is not available
physical impurity

starter: Recite the steps of wudu in order.
Name three things that break wudu.
What does taharah mean?

teach.heading: Why purity matters
bullets: “Allah loves those who repent and those who purify themselves” (2:222)
Cleanliness is part of faith
Purity is required for prayer
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Remind pupils of Qur’an 5:6 from last year. The hadith ‘purification is half of faith’ is in Sahih Muslim. Ask: what are examples of cleanliness in your daily routine?

teach.heading: Wudu in detail
bullets: Fard acts: wash the face, arms to elbows, wipe the head, wash the feet
Sunnah acts: bismillah, siwak, rinsing mouth and nose
Order and washing three times are sunnah
teach.note: Fard actions come directly from 5:6. Madhhabs differ on details such as the niyyah and order; mention that families follow different madhhabs. Pupils check their understanding by correcting an incorrect wudu in a video or script.

teach.heading: Ghusl
bullets: Required after major impurity (janabah)
Also required after menstruation and post-natal bleeding ends
Make intention, wash the body, rinse mouth and nose, ensure water reaches all the body
teach.note: Treat with maturity and brevity; this is standard fiqh for Year 7. Explain that boys and girls study it as part of becoming responsible adults. Use correct terms and direct questions to parents or teachers for more detail.

teach.heading: Tayammum
bullets: Used if water is not available or harmful to use
Strike clean earth with both hands
Wipe the face and the hands
Mentioned in the Qur’an (5:6)
teach.note: Teach as a mercy of Allah. Give a worked scenario: a traveller in the desert, or someone with a skin condition for whom water is harmful. The details of the strikes differ between madhhabs; teach the basic form. Ask: how does tayammum show that Islam is practical?

teach.heading: Conditions of salah

Purity: wudu or ghusl
Covering the awrah
Facing the qiblah and the correct time
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Pupils are at or near the age of responsibility, so tie this to personal duty. The Prophet ﷺ said to pray as you have seen me pray (Bukhari, Malik ibn al-Huwayrith). Reciting al-Fatihah
Ruku’, sujud and sitting between them
Final tashahhud and salam

Longer prayers: stand for the third and fourth

lessons.title: How hadith were preserved: memory, writing and the great collections
lessons.bigQuestion: How could words spoken 1,400 years ago reach us accurately today?
objectives: To understand how the hadith were preserved from the time of the Companions to the great collections
successCriteria: All: name two ways the Companions preserved hadith
Most: put the main stages of preservation in order
Some: explain why the great collections are trusted
lessons.crossCurricular: History: chronology, placing the stages of preservation on a timeline
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the Muslim tradition of scholarship and careful learning

keywords.def: the Companions who met the Prophet ﷺ as believers
memorising
a scholar of hadith
a book that gathers many hadith with their chains
the chain of narrators who passed a hadith on

hook.text: How could words spoken 1,400 years ago reach us accurately today?
hook.a: Through careful memorising, writing, travelling to check, and named chains of trusted narrators, gathered into great books.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ made du'a that Allah brighten the face of the one who hears a hadith from him and passes it on as he heard it (reported by at-Tirmidhi). Passing on knowledge accurately is an act of worship.

starter.q: What is a hadith?
starter.a: A report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did or approved
options: A report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did or approved

starter.q: Fi'l means ...
Which ayah says the Prophet ﷺ was sent to make clear what was revealed?
Give one reason Muslims need the Sunnah.
starter.a: It explains how to carry out the Qur'an, e.g. how to pray

teach.heading: The Companions remembered
bullets: Arabs had strong memories and oral culture
Companions learnt his words carefully
Abu Hurayrah narrated over 5,000 reports
They taught the next generation
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Abu Hurayrah narrated the largest number of hadith. Others well known for narrating many: Abdullah ibn Umar, Anas ibn Malik, Aisha, Abdullah ibn Abbas. Ask: how do you memorise surahs? The same discipline was used for hadith.

teach.heading: Some Companions wrote
bullets: Abdullah ibn Amr wrote hadith with permission
Letters and treaties were written down
Later, travel to check one hadith
Writing and memory checked each other
teach.note: Abu Dawud reports that Abdullah ibn Amr was told to write, because only truth came from the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Bukhari mentions that Jabir ibn Abdullah travelled a month's journey to hear one hadith from Abdullah ibn Unays. Early on the Prophet ﷺ was careful that the Qur'an was not mixed with other writing; later writing of hadith was widespread.

teach.heading: From notebooks to great books
teach.note: Caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (around 100 AH) asked scholars to gather hadith officially, as al-Bukhari mentions. Al-Bukhari died 256 AH; Muslim died 261 AH. The 'six books' are Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

timeline.label: Lifetime
timeline.text: Companions hear, memorise and some write

timeline.label: c. 100 AH
timeline.text: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz orders gathering

teach.heading: Why are they trusted?
bullets: Every hadith comes with its chain
Narrators' honesty and memory were checked
Bukhari and Muslim: the most authentic books
Scholars still check gradings today
teach.note: Muslim scholars regard Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim as the most authentic books after the Qur'an. Explain that collectors rejected many more reports than they accepted.

check.q: Who ordered the official gathering of hadith around 100 AH?
check.why: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz was the caliph who ordered it. Al-Bukhari and Malik compiled books later; Abu Hurayrah was a Companion who narrated.

practice.q: Put in order: Sahih al-Bukhari; Companions memorise; Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's order; the Followers learn.
practice.a: Companions memorise; the Followers learn; Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's order; Sahih al-Bukhari
practice.model: I do: the Companions heard him first, so they come first. The Followers (Tabi'un) learnt from them. Around 100 AH the caliph ordered gathering. Al-Bukhari wrote his Sahih in the 3rd century.

practice.q: Which Companion narrated the most hadith?
Name the two most authentic hadith books.

independent.q: Make a five-stage timeline of how hadith were preserved, with one sentence per stage, in the pupil PDF or portal response box.
independent.a: Companions (memory, some writing); Followers; Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's order; early books such as the Muwatta'; the great collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim.
independent.model: Teacher completes stage 1: 'The Companions heard the Prophet ﷺ, memorised his words and some, such as Abdullah ibn Amr, wrote them down.'

independent.q: Extend: explain why travelling to check one hadith shows how careful the early Muslims were.
independent.a: They wanted to hear it directly from the narrator to be sure of every word, not rely on rumours.

independent.q: Stretch: why do you think a chain of names makes a report more trustworthy?
independent.a: Each person can be checked for honesty and memory, so a fake or mistaken link can be found.

exit.q: Sahih al-Bukhari was written in which century AH?
exit.a: The 3rd

exit.q: Back to our ponder: how did words from 1,400 years ago reach us accurately?
exit.a: Memory, writing, checking narrators, chains and great collections.

lessons.bigQuestion: If you hear 'someone said that someone said ...', how do you decide whether to believe it?

keywords.def: the chain of narrators who passed a hadith on
the actual words of the hadith
a person who passes on a hadith
uprightness: the narrator is honest and pious
precision: the narrator remembers or writes accurately

hook.text: If you hear 'someone said that someone said ...', how do you decide whether to believe it?
hook.a: You check who passed it on, whether they are honest and accurate, and whether the chain is complete: exactly what isnad checking does.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who believe, if a wrongdoer brings you news, verify it' (al-Hujurat 49:6). The scholars of hadith applied this by checking every person in the chain.

starter.q: Who ordered the official gathering of hadith?
Which Companion narrated the most hadith?
Name one of the six books of hadith.
starter.a: Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i or Ibn Majah

starter.q: Sunnah means ...
starter.a: The way of the Prophet ﷺ

teach.heading: Two parts of every hadith
bullets: Isnad: the chain of people
Matn: the words reported
Both are checked by scholars
'The isnad is part of the religion'
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: 'The isnad is part of the religion; were it not for the isnad, anyone could say whatever they wished.' This is recorded in the introduction of Sahih Muslim.

teach.heading: A real chain: Bukhari's first hadith
teach.note: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 1, on intentions. Read the chain down to the matn. Each arrow is a person who heard from the one above.

timeline.label: Alqamah
timeline.text: from Umar ibn al-Khattab, from the Prophet ﷺ

teach.heading: Checking the narrators
bullets: 'Adalah: honest, upright, practising
Dabt: accurate memory or careful writing
Did they actually meet? Chain connected
Whole books were written about narrators
teach.note: Scholars wrote books of biographies of narrators ('ilm ar-rijal): dates of birth and death, teachers, students and reliability. If two people could not have met, the chain is broken.

check.q: A narrator is honest but often forgets and mixes up words. What is the problem?
check.why: Honesty ('adalah) is fine; accuracy (dabt) is weak. Both are needed. The length of the matn is not the issue.

teach.heading: Checking the matn
bullets: Does it agree with the Qur'an?
Does it agree with stronger hadith?
Is there a hidden defect?
Exaggerated or odd claims are a warning
teach.note: Scholars also examined the text: contradiction with stronger evidence or a hidden defect ('illah) could weaken a report even with a good-looking chain.

practice.q: Label the isnad and matn: 'Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: the prayer in congregation is better than prayer alone by twenty-seven degrees.'
practice.a: Isnad: Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar. Matn: 'the prayer in congregation is better than prayer alone by twenty-seven degrees.' (Bukhari and Muslim)
practice.model: I do: underline every name and 'from': that is the isnad. Box the words after 'said': that is the matn. Check: does the chain reach the Prophet ﷺ? Yes, through Ibn Umar.

practice.q: Which quality is about honesty?
Which ayah tells believers to verify news?

independent.q: Chain detective (pupil PDF): three made-up practice chains. For each, say if it is connected and if each narrator has 'adalah and dabt, then decide 'reliable' or 'not reliable'.
independent.a: Chain A: connected, all reliable: reliable. Chain B: two narrators who never met: broken, not reliable. Chain C: one narrator known for lying: not reliable.
independent.model: Teacher does Chain A with the class: check each link met, check each narrator's description, then decide.

independent.q: Extend: explain Ibn al-Mubarak's words 'the isnad is part of the religion'.
independent.a: Without chains anyone could invent sayings; the chain protects the religion from lies.

independent.q: Stretch: how can you apply isnad thinking to a message forwarded on a phone?
independent.a: Ask who first said it, whether they are reliable, and whether there is a real source before sharing (49:6).

exit.q: The matn is ...
exit.a: The words of the hadith

exit.q: Back to our ponder: how do you decide whether to believe 'someone said that someone said'?
exit.a: Check every person in the chain for honesty and accuracy and that the chain is connected.

Dabt means ...
Who said 'the isnad is part of the religion'?
Which ayah tells us to verify news?

teach.heading: Five conditions of sahih
bullets: 1. The chain is connected
2. Every narrator is upright ('adl)
3. Every narrator is precise (dabt)
4. No irregularity against stronger narrators
5. No hidden defect ('illah)
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. These are the five conditions as defined by the scholars of hadith (for example Ibn as-Salah). Ask pupils to link 2 and 3 to last lesson.

teach.heading: Four main grades
teach.note: Hasan is accepted and acted upon like sahih. Da'if is not used to establish rulings; mawdu' is not a hadith at all, so it must never be attributed to the Prophet ﷺ.

head: Grade
Meaning
Used for rulings?
rows: Weak: a problem in chain or narrator

teach.heading: Sort the reports
teach.note: These are teaching descriptions, not real hadith. Discuss each card.

cards: A. Connected chain of upright, precise narrators
B. A narrator known for lying
C. A gap of two generations in the chain
D. Upright narrators, one slightly less precise
E. A 'quote' with no chain at all
F. Narrators who never met each other

teach.heading: Before you share
bullets: Ask: which collection? Which number?
Check the grading on a trusted site or with a teacher
No source? Do not say 'the Prophet ﷺ said'
Better to say nothing than to lie
teach.note: Teach a habit: 'Source, grade, then share.' Many popular online 'hadith' have no source. Pupils can say 'I read that ...' rather than attributing it.

check.q: A narrator in the chain is known as a liar. The report is ...
check.why: A liar breaks the condition of uprightness, so the report is rejected. Sounding nice is not evidence.

practice.q: A friend posts: 'The Prophet ﷺ said: seek knowledge even as far as China.' No collection is given. What should you do?
practice.a: Do not share it as a hadith. Scholars graded this report as very weak or fabricated. Explain kindly and share an authentic hadith on knowledge instead.
practice.model: I do: 1) Is there a collection and number? No. 2) Check with a teacher or trusted source: scholars of hadith grade this report as very weak or fabricated. 3) So I must not say 'the Prophet ﷺ said'. 4) Reply kindly with an authentic alternative.

practice.q: Which grade is a fabricated report?
Can a da'if hadith establish a ruling?

independent.q: Write a short guide in the portal response box: 'Five checks before you share a hadith online.' Start: 'Check 1: ...'
independent.a: Ask for the collection and number; check the grading; check with a teacher; do not attribute without a source; remember the warning about lying about the Prophet ﷺ.
independent.model: Teacher writes check 1: 'Check 1: Find the source. A real hadith names its collection, such as Sahih al-Bukhari, and its number.'

independent.q: Extend: explain the difference between da'if and mawdu'.
independent.a: Da'if is weak, with a problem in the chain; mawdu' is a lie, not from the Prophet ﷺ at all.

independent.q: Stretch: why is the fifth condition (no hidden defect) needed if the chain looks fine?
independent.a: A chain can look good but experts may find a hidden fault, for example a narrator mixing two reports.

exit.q: How many conditions must a sahih hadith meet?
exit.a: Five

exit.q: Back to our ponder: why is a fake quote of the Prophet ﷺ so serious?
exit.a: It changes the religion and he warned that whoever lies about him deliberately takes his seat in the Fire.

lessons.homework: Teach someone at home the four grades of hadith and the five checks, and write down one question they asked.
lessons.send: SEND: two-column sort with picture cues (tick and cross). EAL: grade names with simple meanings. Stretch: find out who Ibn as-Salah was.

lessons.title: Ikhlas in daily life: guarding and renewing our intentions
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it possible to do something good and still lose the reward for it? How?
objectives: To understand how Muslims protect sincerity before, during and after an action
successCriteria: All: name two things that spoil sincerity
Most: describe how to check intention before, during and after a deed
Some: give advice to someone worried about showing off
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: self-reflection and the inner life

keywords.def: sincerity: doing a deed for Allah alone
showing off: doing good so that people praise you
intention: the purpose in the heart
the heart
turning back to Allah and asking forgiveness

hook.text: Is it possible to do something good and still lose the reward for it? How?
hook.a: Yes: by showing off (riya'), or by boasting about it or reminding people of it afterwards (2:264).

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah does not look at your forms or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds' (Muslim).

starter.q: Finish: 'Actions are only by ...'
What does riya' mean?
Which ayah says believers were commanded to worship Allah sincerely?
Is a good intention enough to make a wrong action right?
starter.a: No: the action must also be correct

teach.heading: Allah looks at hearts
bullets: Not looks or money, but hearts and deeds
Sincerity is hidden: only Allah sees it
Small deeds with ikhlas can be great
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Hadith in Muslim. Ask: why might a small, hidden deed be worth more than a big, public one?

teach.heading: Before, during and after
teach.note: Walk through the cycle with one example: reading Qur'an.
cycle: Before: set the intention for Allah
During: keep it sincere if people watch
After: do not boast or remind people
If it slips: make tawbah and renew

teach.heading: Things that spoil a deed
bullets: Riya': doing it to be seen
Boasting about it afterwards
Reminding people of a favour (2:264)
Doing it only for worldly gain
teach.note: Al-Baqarah 2:264: do not cancel your charity by reminders of generosity or by injury. The Prophet ﷺ called riya' 'the minor shirk' (reported by Ahmad).

check.q: Zara gives sadaqah, then keeps reminding her cousin about it. What does 2:264 say?
options: She should give more next time
check.why: 2:264 warns that reminders of generosity and hurt cancel charity. Giving more does not fix the intention problem.

teach.heading: Do not stop doing good
bullets: Shaytan whispers: 'you're showing off, so stop'
Keep doing good; fix the intention
Hidden deeds build sincerity
Make du'a for ikhlas
teach.note: Scholars warn that stopping good deeds for fear of people is itself a trap. The answer is to keep the deed and correct the heart. Encourage one secret good deed each week.

practice.q: Yusuf reads Qur'an beautifully in class and starts enjoying the praise. What should he do?
practice.a: Keep reading, renew his intention for Allah, thank Allah for the gift, make du'a for ikhlas, and do some recitation privately too.
practice.model: I do: 1) Name the danger: enjoying praise can lead to riya'. 2) Do not stop the good deed. 3) Renew the niyyah: 'I recite for Allah.' 4) Add hidden recitation at home. 5) Make du'a for sincerity.

practice.q: Which is a hidden deed?
practice.a: Praying two rak'ahs alone at night
options: Praying two rak'ahs alone at night
Posting a photo of your charity

independent.q: Write an advice column reply in the portal response box to 'Worried Wafiq': 'Whenever I do something good I wonder if I'm showing off. Should I stop?' Start: 'Dear Wafiq, ...'
independent.a: Says do not stop; renew intention; hidden deeds; du'a; hadith that Allah looks at hearts; tawbah if the heart slips.
independent.model: Teacher writes the opening: 'Dear Wafiq, the fact that you worry about your intention is a good sign. Do not stop doing good, because ...'

independent.q: Extend: plan one secret good deed for this week and how you will keep it secret.
independent.a: For example: making du'a for a classmate by name every night; putting coins in a charity box without telling anyone.

independent.q: Stretch: why did the Prophet ﷺ call riya' 'minor shirk'?
independent.a: Because the person does worship partly for people, giving others a share of what should be for Allah alone.

exit.q: What should you do if your intention slips?
exit.a: Make tawbah and renew it

exit.q: Back to our ponder: how can a good deed lose its reward?
exit.a: Showing off, boasting or reminding people of it.

lessons.homework: Do your secret good deed and write a two-line reflection (without saying what the deed was).
lessons.send: SEND: the four-step cycle as a card to keep. EAL: word bank. Stretch: read 2:262-264 in translation and summarise.

lessons.title: How to explain a hadith: narrator, meaning and lessons
lessons.bigQuestion: If you had to explain a hadith to a younger child, what would you need to tell them first?
objectives: To understand how to explain a hadith clearly, as scholars do, using its source, meaning and lessons
successCriteria: All: name the source and narrator of a hadith
Most: explain the key words and the main meaning
Some: draw two lessons and apply them to life today
lessons.crossCurricular: English (Year 7 non-fiction): writing an explanation with clear structure and evidence
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the tradition of explaining hadith (sharh)

keywords.def: an explanation of a text
benefits or lessons from a text
the actual words of the hadith
the chain of narrators who passed a hadith on
the situation in which something was said

hook.text: If you had to explain a hadith to a younger child, what would you need to tell them first?
hook.a: Who said it and who narrated it, where it is found, what the words mean, and what lessons it teaches.

islamicLink.text: Allah says the Prophet ﷺ was sent 'so that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them' (an-Nahl 16:44). Explaining his words carefully continues this work of making things clear.

starter.q: Zakah on £1,000 above the nisab is ...
Name the five pillars in the order of Ibn Umar's hadith.
Which narrator is the son of Umar ibn al-Khattab?
What does riya' mean?

teach.heading: Five steps to explain a hadith
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. This is how commentaries (sharh) are organised. Pupils will use these steps in Years 10 and 11 for the set passages.

teach.heading: Worked example
teach.note: Model the five steps on the five pillars hadith, thinking aloud.

model.problem: Explain the hadith 'Islam is built on five'.
steps: Source: Bukhari and Muslim, so sahih
Narrator: Abdullah ibn Umar, a Companion
Words: 'built' pictures Islam as a building; 'five' are its pillars
Meaning: these five acts are the essential base of Islam
Lessons: never neglect a pillar; build other good deeds on top
model.answer: A clear explanation follows source, narrator, words, meaning, lessons.

teach.heading: Good and poor explanations
teach.note: Discuss what makes the right side stronger.

teach.heading: Careful explaining
bullets: Explain only what you know
Use scholars' explanations, not guesses
Say 'Allah knows best' when unsure
Never add words to a hadith
teach.note: Adab of knowledge: a student does not invent meanings. 'Allahu a'lam' (Allah knows best) is a sign of knowledge, not weakness.

check.q: Which step answers 'Where is this hadith found and is it reliable?'
check.why: The source step names the collection and its grade. The narrator step is about who reported it.

practice.q: Use the five steps on the hadith on intentions (as a class).
practice.a: Source: Bukhari and Muslim, sahih. Narrator: Umar ibn al-Khattab. Words: niyyah, hijrah. Meaning: deeds are valued by the intention behind them. Lessons: check intentions; turn habits into worship.
practice.model: I do the first two steps: 'Source: this hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, so it is sahih. Narrator: Umar ibn al-Khattab.' Pupils do steps 3 to 5 on whiteboards.

practice.q: Which step is 'Never neglect salah'?

independent.q: Explain this hadith using the five steps in the portal response box: 'None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself' (Bukhari and Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik).
independent.a: Source: Bukhari and Muslim, sahih. Narrator: Anas ibn Malik. Words: 'truly believes' means complete iman; 'brother' includes fellow Muslims. Meaning: complete faith includes wanting good for others. Lessons: share, be happy for others' success, avoid envy.
independent.model: Teacher completes step 1 and step 2 with the class first, then pupils continue from step 3.

independent.q: Extend: add a sentence on how this hadith could change behaviour in a school.
independent.a: For example: helping a classmate understand work instead of keeping tips to myself.

independent.q: Stretch: what does 'truly believes' tell us about iman?
independent.a: Iman has levels: a person can be a believer without complete iman; actions and feelings increase it.

exit.q: The first step in explaining a hadith is ...
exit.a: Source

exit.q: Back to our ponder: what do you tell a child first when explaining a hadith?
exit.a: Where it comes from and who narrated it, then the meaning and lessons.

lessons.homework: Explain one hadith you know to someone at home using the five steps, and write down your explanation.
lessons.send: SEND: five-step card with sentence starters. EAL: key word list for the Anas hadith. Stretch: explain the hadith of the strong believer (Muslim) using the steps.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Say: if you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive your sins' (Al Imran 3:31). Learning the Sunnah well is a way of following the Prophet ﷺ out of love.

starter.q: Hadith or Sunnah: which is the report?
Who said 'the isnad is part of the religion'?
How many conditions for a sahih hadith?
Zakah on £800 above the nisab?

teach.heading: The big picture
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Build the concept map together; ask pupils to add a fact to each branch in the chat.

teach.heading: Common mix-ups
teach.note: Address the three most common errors from the half term.

head: Mix-up
Correct
rows: Umar: intentions hadith. Ibn Umar: five pillars hadith
Hadith: the report. Sunnah: the way

teach.heading: Answering 'explain' questions
bullets: Point: answer the question
Evidence: ayah or hadith with source
Explain: what it shows
Link: back to the question
teach.note: Model on screen: 'Explain why Muslims check the isnad.'

model.problem: Explain why Muslims check the isnad of a hadith.
steps: Point: to make sure a report really comes from the Prophet ﷺ
Explain: checking each narrator's honesty and accuracy exposes mistakes and lies
Link: so Muslims follow only what is authentic
model.answer: A developed PEEL paragraph with a reference.

teach.heading: Quick check: who narrated it?
bullets: Umar ibn al-Khattab: intentions
Abdullah ibn Umar: five pillars
Anas ibn Malik: love for your brother
teach.note: Poll, then ask pupils to explain the difference between Umar and his son Abdullah.

check.q: Which hadith did Abdullah ibn Umar narrate?
check.why: Ibn Umar narrated the five pillars hadith. The intentions hadith is from his father, Umar; 'none of you truly believes' is from Anas.

practice.q: Write a PEEL paragraph: 'Explain why the Sunnah is important.'
practice.a: Point: it explains the Qur'an. Evidence: 16:44 or 4:80. Explain: e.g. salah details. Link: Muslims need it to practise Islam.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: the Sunnah is important because it shows how to put the Qur'an into practice. Evidence: Allah says the Prophet ﷺ was sent to make clear what was revealed (16:44). Explain: for example, the Qur'an commands prayer, but the Sunnah shows how to pray. Link: so without the Sunnah Muslims could not practise Islam fully.'

practice.q: Fill the gap: a hadith with a liar in its chain is ...

independent.a: Answers from the unit: definitions, narrators, grades, conditions, pillars, ayat 4:80, 16:44, 49:6, 98:5.
independent.model: Teacher answers box 1 aloud from memory first, then shows how to check and correct in a second colour.

independent.q: Extend: write a PEEL paragraph: 'Explain why intentions matter in Islam.'
independent.a: Point, the intentions hadith with source, example, link.

independent.q: Stretch: 'Muslims should only ever share hadith that are sahih.' Give one reason to agree and one point to consider.
independent.a: Agree: lying about the Prophet ﷺ is very serious. Consider: hasan hadith are also accepted; the key is to share only what scholars accept and to cite the source.

review and revision

starter.q: Taqrir means ...
What did Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz order?
Which grade is fabricated?

teach.heading: Quiz rules
bullets: Bismillah and du'a first
Read each question twice
Answer every question
No notes; your own work

teach.heading: Going through answers
bullets: Mark in a different colour
Write WHY the right answer is right
Note which topics you missed

check.q: Re-check: which part of a hadith is 'from Nafi', from Ibn Umar'?
check.why: Names linked by 'from' are the chain (isnad). The matn is the words; sharh is an explanation.

teach.heading: Reflect and set a target
bullets: One thing I now know well
One thing to revisit
One action this week
teach.note: Targets must be precise: not 'revise more' but 'learn the five conditions of sahih by Friday'. Spring 2 is the fiqh of worship: purity and salah.

practice.q: Practice question before the quiz: 'Give two ways the Companions preserved hadith.'
practice.a: Memorising; writing (e.g. Abdullah ibn Amr); teaching others; travelling to check.
practice.model: I do: 'One way was memorising: the Companions learnt his words by heart. Another was writing: Abdullah ibn Amr wrote hadith with permission.'
